findings.runup_tempo: unknown (not provided), but long ground contact (200 ms) suggests a more deliberate, controlled approach rather than a high-momentum sprint.
findings.back_leg_mechanics: back knee 157° at BFC indicates partial flexion—adequate load absorption but could generate more drive if extended closer to 160–165°.
findings.front_leg_brace: excellent; 173° front-knee angle shows strong braking and energy transfer into trunk and arm.
findings.hip_shoulder_separation: 44.5° at FFC — moderate; earlier shoulder rotation may be reducing torque potential.
findings.lateral_flexion: −40.5° lateral tilt is excessive contralateral flexion—enhances release height but markedly increases lumbar stress risk.
findings.release_height: 2.14 m (≈1.16 × height) — significantly above average, reflecting tall posture and strong front-leg block.
findings.temporal_patterning: BFC→release = 0.27 s, FFC→release = 0.07 s — efficient transfer, though the short FFC window suggests rapid arm acceleration after front-foot strike.
findings.arm_position: ‘above shoulder’ at FFC aligns with high-arm side-on release, consistent with classical seam bowler mechanics.

drills: rotational medicine-ball throws to enhance hip–shoulder separation timing
side-plank and bird-dog progressions for lumbar control under lateral load
single-leg drop landings to reduce BFC contact duration and improve reactivity
high-knee bounding drills to promote quicker transition from BFC to FFC
overhead bowling release drills emphasizing upright posture and delayed side flexion
watchouts: lateral flexion exceeding 35° greatly increases lumbar shear; prioritize trunk symmetry work
avoid premature shoulder rotation before full front-foot brace
consider shortening BFC contact (currently ~200 ms) to increase momentum carry-through
ensure hip–shoulder decoupling for maximal kinetic storage
